subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Representativeness Heuristic
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Representativeness Heuristic.

hook.text: Linda is 31, outspoken, and studied philosophy. Is she more likely a bank teller—or a feminist bank teller?

buildup.text: Most people say feminist bank teller. But that's logically impossible—it's a subset of all bank tellers.

discovery.text: We judge probability by resemblance. Linda 'looks like' a feminist, so we ignore base rates entirely.

twist.text: Even statisticians fall for this. Narrative fit overrides mathematical logic in the human mind.

climax.text: Tversky and Kahneman showed that we confuse 'sounds right' with 'is probable' across countless domains.

punchline.text: A good story beats good math—in your brain.

quiz.question: What is the conjunction fallacy?
options: Judging a specific combo as more likely than its parts

details.summary: The representativeness heuristic judges probability by resemblance to a stereotype. A quiet, bookish person seems more likely to be a librarian than a salesperson, even though salespeople vastly outnumber librarians. This heuristic ignores base rates and produces conjunction fallacies.
details.whyItMatters: Representativeness leads people to ignore statistical reality in favor of how well something matches a mental category. It explains many intuitive probability errors.
takeaways: Probability is judged by resemblance to a category prototype
The conjunction fallacy arises from representativeness

faq.question: What is the conjunction fallacy?
faq.answer: People judge a specific combination as more likely than one of its components alone. The classic example: Linda is more likely to be a feminist bank teller than just a bank teller. This is logically impossible since every feminist bank teller is also a bank teller.

faq.question: Why do people ignore base rates?
faq.answer: Base rates are abstract statistics, while descriptions are vivid and narrative. The brain defaults to matching descriptions against category prototypes rather than doing probability math. When a description strongly matches a rare category, base rate information is overwhelmed by resemblance.
